playbook:
When the first season is put to me and I know nothing about the other boats, I take slightly above the posted sustainable share, about 1.25–1.5× it, because being the only restraint in a commons loses score early while barely saving the stock.

When season results are revealed, I compare total landed to the season’s regrowth capacity: if total catch is near or below what lets the stock recover, I stay near the sustainable share; if others crashed the stock, I do not stay virtuous at a collapsed share, I switch to a defensible medium harvest because low absolute takes after a crash leave me behind forever.

When the stock has already fallen and sustainable shares become tiny, I stop treating “sustainable share” as my target and instead target the largest take that leaves next season’s stock comfortably above zero after likely rival catches.

When I am behind on cumulative score with several seasons left, I raise catch in steps rather than all at once, choosing a number that closes part of the gap while holding total expected harvest under the collapse threshold; I avoid jumps large enough to make rivals panic.

When rivals demonstrate restraint for a full season, I reciprocate for one season by taking roughly the group norm, but only if that norm still leaves regrowth positive; restraint is a tool to buy future stock, not a moral default.

When rivals demonstrate greed, I assume future greed until proven otherwise, discount next season’s stock by their likely overharvest, and take my share of the remaining pie before it disappears.

When estimating collapse risk, I mentally subtract plausible rival catches first and then choose my catch so that post-season stock times regrowth still leaves fish for at least one more meaningful season; if that is impossible, the commons is already ending.

When the penultimate season arrives, I shift from preserving the fishery to positioning for extraction: I take enough that, even under aggressive rivals, the final season still contains a worthwhile pool for me to drain.

When the final season arrives, cooperation ends; I take the whole remaining stock minus only the smallest safety buffer needed to avoid accidentally submitting above availability or triggering failure, because nothing after the last season pays for restraint.

When the prompt offers a “sustainable share,” I use it only as a baseline and a signal of stock health, not as a cap; my real cap is driven by horizon, relative score, observed rival behavior, and the zero-stock cliff.

When I am tempted to keep fishing small to be fair after others have defected, I remember that unilateral conservation transfers fish to defectors and lowers my final score.

When I am tempted to grab everything early, I remember that killing the stock early also caps my own total if others back off, so I keep enough alive while any future rounds still matter.

When writing the reply, I give at most one short sentence of cover logic and always end with exactly the required bracket token, since the scoring artifact only credits a parseable submission.

1.text:
On the first season, if I have no information about the other players, I take a large share — up to about a third of the stock — early, since fish taken now are banked no matter what happens later, but I never take so much that the stock collapses even if others are aggressive.

After an early grab, I watch what others did. If they stayed near the sustainable share, I drop to the sustainable share myself to keep the stock regenerating and lock in my accumulation advantage. If they also grabbed, I cut harder — to the sustainable share or below — because the regrowth penalty compounds and everyone loses.

In every middle season, I take exactly the sustainable share. That keeps the stock roughly flat and defuses any incentive for others to race to grab.

I never take more than the sustainable share in middle seasons unless I am clearly losing on total catch and need to make up ground; a mid-game grab triggered rivals last time and shrank everyone's future pie.

In the final season, there is no tomorrow: regrowth is worthless. If I am not last, I take the sustainable share only if the stock is low enough that a free-for-all would wipe it anyway; otherwise I take my full third of the stock (one-third of what remains), not merely the sustainable share — this was my mistake, leaving points on the table with a 2.4 take from 21.6 in the last season.

Hard limits I always respect: never submit a catch that, even with maximal rivals' takes, could push the stock to zero mid-game; never take more than one-third of the current stock in any single season.

If the stock has already been hammered low, I switch to pure survival mode: take the sustainable share exactly, because the marginal fish from grabbing are tiny compared to losing all remaining seasons.

When prompted to submit, I state one short reason and always end the reply with the bracketed [catch: N] token exactly as required.

2.text:
When the stock is high and the game is young, I take exactly my sustainable share, even though it feels passive — overshooting early collapses the stock and caps everyone's total, and full cooperation over all seasons beats the mixed outcome I got.

Each new season, before choosing a number, I compute whether stock + regrowth can support the remaining seasons at the sustainable share; I only fish above share when a small deviation leaves the stock comfortably viable for the rest of the game.

When rivals reveal their pattern, I classify them: if everyone fishes sustainably, I match the sustainable share plus a small premium (at most ~50% over) to edge ahead without triggering retaliation or collapse; if rivals repeatedly overfish, I treat the stock as doomed and shift to grabbing a larger share each season rather than sacrificing for a future that won't exist.

I never leave a season taking less than my sustainable share unless the stock is near zero — the regrowth makes the fish free, so under-fishing is pure loss.

In the final season, I take everything safe: roughly a third of the remaining stock (adjusted down if I expect others to oversubscribe), since there is no future to protect.

In the penultimate season, I fish moderately above share only if the projected final-season stock still gives me a worthwhile last grab.

What did not work: opening big while others were near sustainable — it bought a one-season edge but dragged the stock down for five seasons; and alternating between nervous cooperation and moderate pushes with no consistent rule. What worked better: holding roughly to share when the table cooperated, and escalating on the last two seasons. Next time I commit to one rule per phase rather than improvising season to season, and I always end my reply with the bracketed catch token as the last thing I write.
